strengths: The paper offers an original connection between layer-local self-supervised objectives and end-to-end backpropagation. Theorem 3.1 gives a useful exact gradient-equivalence result for deep linear networks under explicit orthonormality, convex-loss, and optimal-feedback assumptions, and the manuscript provides proofs and targeted numerical checks.

The theory motivates concrete algorithmic changes—direct top-layer feedback and spatially dependent projections—rather than remaining purely conceptual. Ablations consistently associate these changes with greater gradient alignment and better downstream accuracy.

The same-network comparisons against BP-CLAPP++ and BP-InfoNCE are compelling: CLAPP++both obtains 81.18%, 79.62%, and 37.78% on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet, respectively, close to the reported backpropagation baselines. Four-seed confidence intervals are provided for the principal new methods and baselines.

The evaluation spans three image datasets, linear networks, nonlinear MLPs, and convolutional networks. It also includes comparisons with DFA and predictive coding, rank constraints on the feedback projections, and gradient-alignment measurements at multiple training stages.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, openly states that the theory does not extend directly to nonlinear networks or normalized Forward-Forward training, and appropriately limits the global-SSL comparison to matched VGG-style baselines rather than claiming parity with state-of-the-art end-to-end SSL. The standard datasets and basic neuroscience framing present no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The exact-equivalence result is very narrow: it requires square orthonormal weights at every update, linear activations, effectively optimal layerwise feedback matrices, and detached reference representations. Ordinary gradient updates do not preserve orthonormality, so the theorem establishes pointwise equality under an imposed condition rather than equivalence of realistic training trajectories.

The discussion sometimes overgeneralizes the theory to Forward-Forward methods. Actual Forward-Forward uses activation normalization and a nonconforming objective, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that Theorem 3.1 has not been extended to that setting. Similarly, Theorem 3.3 only covers a linear loss, batch size one, and semi-orthonormal linear networks; the nonlinear results are empirical extrapolations.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not fully controlled. Several competing numbers are taken from prior papers, while this work changes the augmentation pipeline and trains the linear probe on concatenated representations from multiple layers. Without re-running competitors under this protocol and architecture, the claim of a new local-SSL state of the art is not conclusive.

Spatial dependence appears to greatly enlarge the feedback operators: flattening pooled spatial positions jointly with channels can create very large dense matrices. The manuscript does not report parameter counts, memory, throughput, or compute-matched controls. This omission is especially important given the locality, efficiency, and biological-plausibility motivation and the use of four A100 GPUs.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite a useful appendix. No code or availability statement is given, and important details are missing, including augmentation magnitudes, linear-probe duration and model selection, exact negative sampling, feedback-matrix shapes/initialization/regularization, and whether all baselines received equal tuning. The main confidence intervals use only four runs, while literature baselines have no harmonized uncertainty.

The biological and resource-efficiency conclusions are stronger than the evidence. Dense spatial projections and direct feedback from the final layer require substantial nonlocal communication, and the claimed memory advantage is not measured or balanced against the storage cost of the feedback matrices. These issues reduce the reach of an otherwise promising and technically interesting contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question and offers a useful common notation connecting several contrastive local-learning methods.

The exact-equivalence result for deep linear networks is conceptually interesting, and the manuscript clearly states restrictive assumptions such as linearity, orthonormal square weights, unconstrained feedback matrices, and instantaneous optimization of those matrices.

The progression from theory to direct feedback and spatially dependent projections is coherent. Gradient-alignment experiments and ablations generally support the qualitative claim that these modifications improve alignment and downstream accuracy.

On CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, the proposed variants achieve performance comparable to the paper's matched backpropagation baselines over four seeds. The work poses little direct societal risk, and the authors do not conceal the limitations of the backpropagation baselines.
weaknesses: The headline claim that local learning “matches” backpropagation is overstated. On STL-10, CLAPP++both obtains 79.62±0.28, versus 80.36±0.26 for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97±1.23 for BP-InfoNCE; the reported 95% confidence intervals do not overlap. Evidence is also limited to one relatively small VGG-style architecture and three modest vision benchmarks.

The claimed local-SSL state of the art is not established through controlled comparisons. Several competing numbers are copied from prior papers, while the proposed method changes augmentation, uses concatenated representations from multiple layers, and may use different architectures or evaluation protocols. Reimplementations under a common protocol are needed.

The practical method introduces potentially enormous spatially dependent projection matrices. From Table A2, an early CIFAR-10 representation can retain 8×8×128 coordinates after pooling, implying a dense projection on thousands of features if implemented as described. The paper does not report projection parameter counts, memory, computation, communication cost, or scaling behavior. This omission is especially consequential because efficiency and biological locality motivate the work.

Direct feedback from the final layer is nonlocal at the network level, and the spatial projections appear to connect broad sets of positions and channels. Calling the resulting method simply “local” therefore needs a precise locality definition and a more careful treatment of transport, wiring, and credit-signal assumptions. The biological-plausibility conclusions are substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

The theoretical equivalence applies only to a degenerate regime: deep linear networks with equal widths and orthonormal weights, plus feedback matrices at their exact optima. These conditions are neither maintained nor approximated during the nonlinear experiments. Theorem 3.1 also names Forward-Forward as an example despite the paper later acknowledging that normalization prevents the theorem from applying; its listed loss is not convex under the theorem's stated assumptions.

The quantity in Definition 3.4 is described as a theoretical upper bound or “optimal local” update, but it only minimizes an activation-gradient MSE within one chosen parameterization. It is not shown to maximize weight-gradient cosine similarity or to upper-bound all local learning rules, so the closeness-to-optimum conclusion is unsupported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code or availability statement, and important details such as the exact dimensions and parameterization of every spatial projection, classifier training duration and regularization, model-selection procedure, and full hyperparameter choices are missing. Several ablations are single reported values, while only selected main results include four-seed uncertainty.

The limitations and impact discussion does not adequately address the method's scaling costs, the fairness of cross-paper comparisons, the narrow experimental scope, or the speculative nature of the neuroscience interpretation. Overall, the core idea is promising, but the current evidence does not reliably support the paper's strongest performance, efficiency, optimality, and biological-locality claims.

strengths: The manuscript presents an original and potentially important connection between local self-supervised learning and end-to-end backpropagation. The theory leads to concrete algorithmic modifications rather than remaining purely explanatory: spatially dependent projections and direct feedback both improve gradient alignment, and the ablations indicate that spatial dependence supplies the largest performance gain.

The empirical results are encouraging across CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny ImageNet. CLAPP++both obtains 81.18%, 79.62%, and 37.78%, respectively, substantially improving the authors' no-spatial-dependence variant and performing near the matched BP-CLAPP++ baseline.

The paper triangulates its argument using proofs, controlled linear-network simulations, gradient-alignment measurements in nonlinear networks, downstream linear evaluation, and comparisons with direct feedback alignment and predictive coding.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The common notation usefully unifies several local-SSL rules, figures communicate the main mechanism well, and the appendix provides proofs, architectures, data augmentations, optimization settings, and confidence intervals over four runs.

The authors appropriately acknowledge several limitations, including the linear and orthonormal assumptions of the exact result, the absence of a theorem for normalized Forward-Forward networks, the non-state-of-the-art nature of the global BP baseline, and the lack of a resource-efficiency analysis. The work presents no substantial research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The exact theory has limited direct applicability. Theorem 3.1 holds only at network states with square orthonormal weights, linear activations, and an optimized or specially fixed projection; ordinary training does not preserve these conditions. The nonlinear CNN method is therefore theory-inspired rather than theoretically justified.

Some necessary assumptions are insufficiently explicit in the theorem statements and proofs. The equivalence uses a relationship between layerwise references such as c^L=(W^L...W^{l+1})c^l and appears to treat the reference branch as stop-gradient, but these conditions are not clearly stated. The text also invokes strict convexity in the proof while stating only convexity of f; strictness actually depends on the positive quadratic regularizer.

The state-of-the-art local-SSL claim is not fully controlled. Several competing numbers are imported from prior papers, whereas CLAPP++ uses SimCLR augmentations and concatenated representations from multiple layers. Without reimplementing strong baselines under the same architecture, augmentations, compute budget, and readout protocol, the table does not isolate the learning rule as the source of the advantage.

The claim that local learning “matches” BP-SSL is slightly overstated. On STL-10, CLAPP++both reaches 79.62±0.28 versus 80.36±0.26 for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97±1.23 for BP-InfoNCE. These results are close and practically meaningful, but not equivalent under the reported intervals.

The evaluation remains limited to a six-layer VGG-style network and relatively small image benchmarks. Experiments on deeper or modern architectures and larger datasets are needed to establish scalability and broader significance.

Reproducibility is only moderate: no code or artifact availability statement is provided, and details such as linear-probe duration and selection protocol, complete CIFAR-10/Tiny-ImageNet splits, projection initialization, parameter counts, and some optimizer settings are missing. The spatially dependent projections may add substantial parameter, memory, communication, or compute costs, but these are not quantified.

The biological-plausibility and efficiency discussion is stronger than the evidence. Direct feedback requires access to a final-layer representation, and spatially indexed feedback can be expensive; neither the physical implementation nor the claimed memory advantage is experimentally evaluated. These limitations should be made more prominent.

strengths: Soundness: The paper gives a coherent theoretical bridge between local contrastive learning and end-to-end BP-SSL. Theorem 3.1 establishes exact gradient equivalence under clearly stated linearity, orthonormality, and optimized-feedback assumptions; Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.5 then motivate direct feedback and spatially dependent projections. The numerical gradient-alignment experiments systematically remove assumptions and broadly support the predicted trends.

Significance: CLAPP++ substantially improves the authors' non-spatial baseline across CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet. Its best variants are practically close to matched VGG-based BP-SSL baselines on the first three datasets, addressing an important gap for local self-supervised learning.

Originality: The common formulation of several contrastive local rules and the use of BP-gradient equivalence to derive spatial projections and direct feedback constitute a novel and productive perspective, rather than merely another empirical local loss.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, connects the theoretical progression to the algorithmic ablations, and candidly states that the exact theorem does not extend to nonlinear networks and that the experiments lag modern ResNet-scale SSL.
Ethics and limitations: The application is low risk, and the authors appropriately discuss architecture and scaling limitations without using that discussion to excuse the empirical gap.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: The exact result depends on highly restrictive conditions—linear networks, square orthonormal weights, unconstrained feedback matrices, and feedback optimized to its loss minimum. In the numerical verification, the feedback matrix is optimized to convergence separately on each fixed batch. This is substantially different from ordinary stochastic SSL, where one shared feedback matrix is updated online, so the theorem provides limited support for the practical CLAPP++ setting.

There is an important ambiguity between the analysis and implementation. The derivations treat the reference activity c as constant with respect to the feedforward weights, and Equation 8 contains only the target-branch contribution. Algorithm 3, however, computes c^l through the same trainable layer and does not show a stop-gradient on c^l before forming the loss, which would introduce an additional weight-gradient term. The paper must state and implement the detachment convention consistently.

Several central empirical claims are overstated. On STL-10, the best local result is 79.62±0.28 versus 80.36±0.26 for BP-CLAPP++ and 81.97±1.23 for BP-InfoNCE; the confidence intervals with BP-CLAPP++ do not overlap. Thus the statement that the performance margin has 'disappeared' is not supported statistically. On ImageNet, the gap remains large: 44.16 versus 48.52 for BP-CLAPP++ and 55.19 for BP-InfoNCE.

The state-of-the-art comparison mixes published results obtained under potentially different architectures, augmentations, training budgets, and readout protocols. The proposed method concatenates representations from every layer for linear evaluation, which can materially help a layerwise method. Re-running the strongest baselines under the identical architecture, augmentation, and multilayer-readout protocol is needed to substantiate the SOTA claim.

The practical cost story is incomplete. Spatial dependence enlarges B substantially and direct feedback requires top-layer signals at every layer, weakening both the locality and biological-plausibility narrative. Table 3 counts activation storage rather than complete peak GPU memory, appears to omit projection parameters, gradients, and optimizer state, and reports estimates for ideal algorithms that were not used for full training. Consequently, the claimed 38–60% memory benefit is not demonstrated end to end.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The architecture, major optimizer settings, augmentations, and spatial pooling sizes are provided, but the manuscript's 'Code is available at' field is blank, linear-probe duration and selection details are missing, and some loss/projection implementation details remain ambiguous. ImageNet is reported without uncertainty, while most confidence intervals use only four seeds.

Presentation contains several proof-level notation errors or unclear statements, especially in Appendix B.2 (for example, inconsistent V_l versus V_empty terms and expressions described as functions of matrices despite containing gradient-shaped factors). Even if the intended Theorem 3.3 argument can be reconstructed, the proof should be corrected and independently checked.

The impact statement is perfunctory. Although no major ethical concern is apparent, claims about biological plausibility should be qualified more carefully because learned long-range direct feedback and large spatially structured projections are not obviously biologically local.

strengths: The paper asks an important question and offers a useful common notation connecting several local self-supervised learning rules.
The combination of linear-network analysis, gradient-alignment measurements, ablations, and evaluations on four image datasets is broader than typical work on biologically motivated local learning.

Spatially dependent feedback yields substantial empirical improvements over the authors' CLAPP baseline, and the paper clearly acknowledges that its global BP baselines are not state-of-the-art SSL systems.
The manuscript is generally readable, and its low-risk research setting makes the brief ethics statement adequate.
weaknesses: The central equivalence proof appears inconsistent with the stated implementation. The proof differentiates the loss only through z^l and treats c^l as fixed, whereas Algorithm 3 computes c^l with the same trainable layer and does not show a stop-gradient on c^l itself. If gradients flow through this branch, the omitted derivative invalidates the claimed equality; if they do not, this essential assumption must be stated and enforced.

The theoretical guarantees hold only under highly restrictive conditions: linear networks, square orthonormal weights, instantaneously optimized unconstrained feedback matrices, or—in Theorem 3.3—a linear loss and batch size one. The experiments jointly train nonlinear networks and feedback matrices, but no result bridges this large gap.

Proposition 3.5 is primarily an expressivity statement: an unrestricted, all-to-all spatial matrix can reproduce a linear BP operator, and its construction explicitly depends on the forward weights. It neither shows that the local objective will learn that operator nor supports the stronger biological-plausibility interpretation.

The main ablation confounds spatial structure with a very large increase in feedback-matrix capacity. There is no parameter-matched control, structured random-feedback control, or analysis showing that improved accuracy is caused by closer BP alignment rather than simply more parameters.

The claim of matching BP-SSL is supported only against deliberately limited VGG/linear-head baselines with relatively low absolute performance. On ImageNet, CLAPP++ variants remain substantially below both BP baselines, while comparisons called local-SSL state of the art mix results from different architectures and protocols.

Resource claims are not established end to end. The reported VRAM values estimate activation storage and omit the potentially large spatial feedback matrices, their gradients, and optimizer states; the memory-efficient ideal algorithms were not used for the benchmark training. Thus the claimed practical savings are incomplete.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the central empirical claims: the manuscript does not fully specify projection dimensions and parameter counts, negative-pair sampling, linear-evaluation duration/model selection, or all optimization details. ImageNet results have no repeated-run uncertainty, and the displayed code-availability line contains no accessible link.

The limitations discussion honestly notes the lack of ResNet and larger-scale experiments, but omits more decisive limitations: dense within-layer and top-down connectivity weakens the locality/biological-plausibility claim, additional parameter capacity confounds the ablation, and the theory-to-practice assumptions are unresolved. These soundness and evidential issues outweigh the promising idea.

strengths: Soundness: The central exact-equivalence result is clearly scoped to deep linear networks with square orthonormal weights, convex losses, and either fixed identity or instantaneously optimized feedback matrices. Numerical experiments appropriately verify how alignment deteriorates as these assumptions are removed.

Originality: The paper develops a useful unifying formalism for several contrastive local-learning rules and uses gradient alignment with global self-supervised backpropagation as a principled design criterion. The spatially dependent CLAPP++ construction and its connection to direct feedback are novel and conceptually interesting.

Significance: The empirical gains are substantial within the local-SSL literature. Spatial dependence raises the reported STL-10 accuracy from 75.10% to 78.66%, and the best variants reach 81.18% on CIFAR-10, 79.62% on STL-10, and 37.78% on Tiny-ImageNet, approximately matching the paper's controlled BP-SSL baselines on those datasets.

Evidence: The authors provide useful ablations connecting spatial dependence and direct feedback to both increased gradient alignment and improved downstream accuracy. Results cover CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet, with four-seed 95% confidence intervals for the first three datasets.

Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, distinguishes exact results from empirical approximations, supplies proofs and training details in the appendix, and candidly notes the remaining ImageNet gap and the difficulty of extending the method to residual architectures. Ethics and limitations: The work presents no apparent material research-ethics risk, and its discussion of scaling limitations is appropriate rather than grounds for a penalty.
weaknesses: Soundness and scope: The strongest theorem relies on restrictive and operationally unrealistic conditions—linearity, square orthonormal layers, and feedback matrices assumed to reach their optimum instantaneously. The nonlinear-network case is supported empirically rather than theoretically, so the exact-equivalence result should not be read as explaining practical CLAPP++ directly.

The convolutional existence result permits a full linear operator between flattened feature maps, whereas the practical algorithm uses coarse pooling for tractability. Consequently, the proposition does not establish exactness for the method actually used in the main experiments.

The practical evidence does not fully support an unqualified claim that local SSL “matches” BP-SSL. On ImageNet, CLAPP++DFB reaches 44.16%, below BP-CLAPP++ at 48.52% and BP-InfoNCE at 55.19%; ImageNet results also lack uncertainty estimates.

The state-of-the-art comparison mixes newly run controlled baselines with numbers cited from prior papers, for which architecture, augmentation, optimization, and readout protocols may differ. Moreover, the evaluation concatenates representations from every layer, which may favor layerwise objectives and limits the strength of cross-paper conclusions.

The efficiency claim is preliminary: Table 3 labels activation-storage estimates as peak VRAM, excludes feedback parameters, gradients, optimizer state, and other allocations, and the authors explicitly did not train end-to-end using the proposed memory-saving implementation. Thus the reported 38–60% savings are not demonstrated measurements of full training memory.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The PDF says “Code is available at” but provides no link, while details such as linear-evaluation duration and some ImageNet repetition information are absent. The smaller experiments use only four seeds, and ImageNet appears to use one run.

The biological-plausibility discussion is somewhat overstated. Direct feedback requires broadcasting top-layer activity, while spatially dependent feedback can entail large structured projection matrices; the manuscript does not fully analyze how these pathways would be learned or implemented biologically. These qualifications weaken the broad concluding claim that the method removes the need for contested backpropagation machinery.
